# Semiconductor optical amplifiers and superluminescent LEDs {#sec-soa} [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/{{< var github_user >}}/{{< var repo >}}/blob/main/{{< var subdir >}}/notebooks/soa-sled.ipynb){.colab-link}  Run this chapter's code in Google Colab (no installation). *Slides 152–158 (semiconductor optical amplifiers: travelling-wave and Fabry–Perot types, gain saturation, polarisation-dependent gain, commercial devices) and 159–161 (superluminescent LEDs).* ## Key relations A laser diode below threshold is an amplifier: light that enters one facet leaves the other amplified by the single-pass gain $G_s=e^{(\Gamma g-\alpha_s)L}$. Two versions exist (slides 155–157): * The **travelling-wave (TW) SOA** has anti-reflection coated (and often angled) facets: one pass, broad and smooth gain spectrum (30–60 nm), about 20–30 dB. * The **Fabry–Perot (FP) SOA** keeps reflecting facets: a regenerative amplifier, whose gain is enhanced at the cavity resonances and suppressed between them, $$G_{FP}=\frac{(1-R_1)(1-R_2)G_s}{\left(1-\sqrt{R_1R_2}\,G_s\right)^2+4\sqrt{R_1R_2}\,G_s\sin^2\phi},$$ with $\phi$ the single-pass phase. The gain ripple is $\left[(1+\sqrt{R_1R_2}G_s)/(1-\sqrt{R_1R_2}G_s)\right]^2$. The gain **saturates** when the signal depletes the carriers (slide 155c). For a homogeneously broadened medium, $G=G_0\exp[-(G-1)P_\text{in}/P_\text{sat}]$, and the output at which the gain has dropped by 3 dB, $P_{o,\text{sat}}$, is quoted in datasheets (slide 158). Because the carrier lifetime is ~0.1–1 ns, the SOA gain follows the bit pattern, unlike the EDFA (@sec-edfa): this causes cross-talk between WDM channels, but also enables all-optical wavelength conversion. A **superluminescent LED** (SLED, slides 159–161) is an SOA with no input: spontaneous emission generated at one end is amplified on its way out, with feedback suppressed by angled facets, an absorbing section or AR coatings. The output is bright and directional like a laser but broadband and incoherent like an LED. ## Fabry–Perot versus travelling-wave SOA ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof sa = Inputs.form({ GsdB: Inputs.range([0, 35], {value: 25, step: 0.5, label: "single-pass gain G_s (dB)"}), lR: Inputs.range([-6, -0.5], {value: -3, step: 0.05, label: "log₁₀ facet reflectance R₁ = R₂"}), L: Inputs.range([200, 2000], {value: 500, step: 50, label: "chip length (µm), n_g = 3.6"}) }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false saOut = { const R = 10 ** sa.lR, Gs = 10 ** (sa.GsdB/10), rr = R*Gs, fsr = 299792458/(2*3.6*sa.L*1e-6), data = []; for (let i = 0; i <= 1200; i++) { const f = -2*fsr + 4*fsr*i/1200, phi = Math.PI*f/fsr; data.push({f: f/1e9, G: 10*Math.log10((1 - R)**2*Gs/((1 - rr)**2 + 4*rr*Math.sin(phi)**2))}); } return {data, R, rr, fsr, ripple: rr < 1 ? 20*Math.log10((1 + rr)/(1 - rr)) : Infinity}; } Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 280, x: {label: "frequency offset (GHz)"}, y: {label: "amplifier gain (dB)", grid: true}, marks: [Plot.line(saOut.data, {x: "f", y: "G", stroke: "#2a78d6", strokeWidth: 2}), Plot.ruleY([sa.GsdB], {stroke: "#eb6834", strokeDasharray: "4,3"})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false html`
R Gs = ${saOut.rr.toPrecision(3)} ${saOut.rr >= 1 ? html`≥ 1: the device lases (not an amplifier)` : html`· gain ripple ${saOut.ripple.toFixed(2)} dB · resonance spacing ${(saOut.fsr/1e9).toFixed(1)} GHz · orange: travelling-wave gain Gs`}
` ``` With cleaved facets ($R=0.32$) the chip lases as soon as $G_s>3$ (5 dB). A 25 dB TW amplifier needs $R\lesssim10^{-4}$ for a ripple below 0.5 dB, which no single AR coating achieves: practical SOAs combine AR coatings with angled waveguides (7–10°) and window regions. ::: {#cell-fig-ripple .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} R = np.logspace(-6, -1, 300) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.5)) for GdB in (15, 20, 25, 30): rr = R*10**(GdB/10) ax.semilogx(R, np.where(rr < 1, 20*np.log10((1 + rr)/(1 - rr)), np.nan), label=f"G_s = {GdB} dB") ax.axvspan(1e-4, 1e-3, color=lz.GRID, alpha=0.6, zorder=0) ax.set(xlabel="facet reflectance R", ylabel="gain ripple (dB)", ylim=(0, 15)); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Peak-to-valley gain ripple of an SOA versus facet reflectance for three single-pass gains. The vertical band marks good AR coatings (10⁻⁴–10⁻³).](soa-sled_files/figure-html/fig-ripple-output-1.png){#fig-ripple width=688 height=367} ::: ::: ## Gain saturation (slide 155c) ::: {#cell-fig-soa-sat .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} Pin = np.logspace(-7, -1, 400) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.6)) for G0dB, c in ((20, lz.PALETTE[0]), (25, lz.PALETTE[1])): G0 = 10**(G0dB/10) G = lz.saturated_gain(G0, Pin, 10e-3) Pout = G*Pin ax.plot(lz.dB(Pout/1e-3), lz.dB(G), color=c, label=f"G₀ = {G0dB} dB") i = np.argmin(abs(lz.dB(G) - (G0dB - 3))) ax.plot(lz.dB(Pout[i]/1e-3), lz.dB(G[i]), "o", color=c) print(f"G0 = {G0dB} dB: P_o,sat = {lz.dB(Pout[i]/1e-3):.1f} dBm (formula {lz.dB(10*np.log(2)*G0/(G0 - 2)):.1f} dBm)") ax.set(xlabel="output power (dBm)", ylabel="gain (dB)", xlim=(-20, 20)); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` G0 = 20 dB: P_o,sat = 8.4 dBm (formula 8.5 dBm) G0 = 25 dB: P_o,sat = 8.4 dBm (formula 8.4 dBm) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Gain versus output power of a TW SOA with small-signal gains of 20 and 25 dB (P_sat = 10 mW of the medium), the shape of slide 155c. The circles mark the 3 dB saturated output power P_o,sat ≈ P_sat ln2 · G₀/(G₀ − 2).](soa-sled_files/figure-html/fig-soa-sat-output-2.png){#fig-soa-sat width=698 height=374} ::: ::: The saturated output power hardly depends on the small-signal gain: it is a property of the medium, $P_\text{sat}=h\nu A/(\Gamma a\tau)$ with $a$ the differential gain and $\tau$ the carrier lifetime. A large mode area and a short lifetime raise it; the 8–11 dBm of slide 158 is typical. ::: {#tbl-soa .cell tbl-cap='Slide 158: commercial TW SOAs. The last column converts the bandwidth to THz.' execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} s = pd.DataFrame([(850, 25, 40, 150, 2.2, 8, None, 7), (1310, 22, 45, 250, 2, 10, 7, 0.5), (1550, 20, 35, 200, 2, 11, 6, 0.5)], columns=["λ (nm)", "gain (dB)", "BW (nm)", "I_F (mA)", "V_F (V)", "P_o,sat (dBm)", "NF (dB)", "ΔG_p (dB)"]) s["BW (THz)"] = (lz.c0*s["BW (nm)"]*1e-9/(s["λ (nm)"]*1e-9)**2/1e12).round(1) s["electrical power (mW)"] = s["I_F (mA)"]*s["V_F (V)"] s ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: SOAs have NF ≈ 6–7 dB, worse than EDFAs (inversion is never complete, and the input coupling loss adds directly to the NF), and they need hundreds of mW of electrical power. Their advantages are size, any wavelength from 650 to 1650 nm, and integration with lasers and modulators on InP chips. ## Superluminescent LEDs (slides 159–161) The spontaneous emission generated near the rear of the stripe is amplified along it. Since the gain is largest at the peak, the output spectrum narrows as the gain grows (**gain narrowing**), but it stays far broader than a laser line. ::: {#cell-fig-sled .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} lam = np.linspace(1150e-9, 1470e-9, 800) shape = np.exp(-4*np.log(2)*((lam - 1310e-9)/70e-9)**2) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.6)) for GdB in (0.1, 10, 20, 30): gL = GdB/4.343*shape P = shape*np.expm1(gL)/np.maximum(gL, 1e-9) P /= P.max() w = lam[P >= 0.5]; fw = w[-1] - w[0] ax.plot(lam*1e9, P, label=f"peak gain {GdB:g} dB: FWHM {fw*1e9:.0f} nm, ℓ_c ≈ {1310e-9**2/fw*1e6:.0f} µm") ax.set(xlabel="wavelength (nm)", ylabel="normalised power"); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Output spectrum of a 1310 nm SLED model: spontaneous emission (Gaussian, 70 nm FWHM) amplified by a gain spectrum of the same shape, P(λ) ∝ r_sp(λ)[G(λ) − 1]/g(λ). Increasing the peak single-pass gain narrows the spectrum; the coherence length λ²/Δλ, which sets the axial resolution of optical coherence tomography, grows accordingly.](soa-sled_files/figure-html/fig-sled-output-1.png){#fig-sled width=719 height=374} ::: ::: SLEDs are the light source of fiber-optic gyroscopes and of optical coherence tomography (OCT), where the coherence length $\ell_c\approx\lambda^2/\Delta\lambda$ (Ch. 1) sets the depth resolution: about 10–20 µm for the 40–45 nm SLEDs of slide 159. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Going further - **Pattern effects and wavelength conversion.** Solve $dn/dt=I/eV-n/\tau-\Gamma a(n-n_{tr})P/(h\nu A)$ for a 10 Gb/s on-off signal through an SOA with $\tau=200$ ps. The gain recovers too slowly: the "1" bits after a run of "0"s are amplified more. A continuous probe at another wavelength receives the inverted pattern: this is cross-gain-modulation wavelength conversion. - **Polarisation-dependent gain** (slide 157). Bulk active layers with a nearly square cross section, or tensile-strained QWs that add TM gain, bring $\Delta G_p$ below 0.5 dB (slide 158). - **SOA versus EDFA noise.** Add the input coupling loss (3 dB from fiber to chip) to the intrinsic $2n_{sp}$ with the Friis formula of @sec-edfa-noise, and show why the SOA NF rarely goes below 6 dB. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Complements - M. J. Connelly, *Semiconductor Optical Amplifiers* (Kluwer, 2002). - Kasap, sec. 4.18–4.19; Agrawal, *Fiber-Optic Communication Systems*, sec. 7.2. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. A 1 mm SOA has a single-pass gain of 30 dB. What facet reflectance keeps the ripple below 1 dB? 2. Using the saturation model, at what input power does a 25 dB SOA with $P_\text{sat}=10$ mW lose 1 dB of gain? 3. Why does a FP SOA have a narrower optical bandwidth (per resonance) than a TW SOA, but a higher peak gain? 4. Estimate the OCT axial resolution (in tissue, $n=1.38$) with a 1310 nm SLED of 45 nm FWHM. What spectral width would give 3 µm?
